faqs.question: Is it compulsory to attend the office Ganesh Chaturthi celebration?
faqs.answer: It should not be, but whether it feels that way depends on who invites you. In a study of 37 employees' workplace celebrations, five people named attendance pressure outright and 36 named required personal sacrifices, so the pressure is real even when nobody states a rule. Put "optional" in writing, and send it from the organiser rather than the reporting manager.

faqs.question: How many days should we keep the Ganpati in the office?
faqs.answer: Three is the usual choice. The traditional shortened forms are 1.5, 3, 5 and 7 days against the festival's full ten, and three fits inside one working week without leaving anyone responsible for the idol over a weekend.

faqs.question: Who should pay for an office Ganesh Chaturthi celebration?
faqs.answer: The company, if you want declining to be genuinely free. A company budget is the only model with no contribution sheet, so nobody has to refuse in front of a list — which is a different and more exposed act than quietly not attending.

faqs.question: Is 14 September 2026 a holiday for offices in India?
faqs.answer: It varies, and you should check rather than assume. Whether it is a working day depends on your state's own notification and your employer's leave policy rather than on any single national rule, so look at both your state list and your HR calendar.

faqs.question: What do we do about colleagues who do not celebrate Ganesh Chaturthi?
faqs.answer: Treat inclusion as a design constraint rather than a disclaimer. Exclusion was the second most-cited complaint in that workplace-celebration study, at 20 of 105 negative responses, and the quote was about invitation lists. Say what the festival is rather than assuming it, and give the ritual a fixed start and end time so not attending just means arriving later.

faqs.question: How can remote employees take part in the office celebration?
faqs.answer: Run the aarti on a video call at a time that suits the furthest timezone, then give everyone something they can open on their own afterwards. A hybrid version where most people are in a room and a few are on a screen is the worst option for those few — the asymmetry does more damage than the distance.

faqs.question: Is a video-call aarti worse than being in the room?
faqs.answer: For group closeness, probably. For the colleague who would rather not be counted, it is better: an online celebration is flatter, and nobody can see who skipped. One published model argues that this general neutrality can work in a minority group member's favour, though it is a proposition rather than a tested result.

faqs.question: Do we need to take a collection from everyone?
faqs.answer: No, and there is a good reason not to. A contribution sheet is a public document, so a per-head collection makes the opt-out visible to the whole team. If you must collect, use a closed envelope so nobody can audit who said no.

faqs.question: When should we start planning the office celebration?
faqs.answer: Earlier than feels necessary. Across 89 SubhSandesh rakhi pages the median lead time was zero days and not one was built more than seven days ahead, so anything that needs other people's diaries — a call slot, a timezone, prasad by courier — is exactly what fails at the last minute.

faqs.question: Can we send one Ganesh Chaturthi page to the whole company?
faqs.answer: You can, but it is the wrong tool for that job. A personalised page is a one-to-one object — 42.0% of creators password-protect one before sharing it, which means nothing on a link pasted to four hundred people. Use it for the handful of people you would have written to individually.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Ganesh Chaturthi Celebration in Office: Who Comes, Who Pays

Settle three things before anyone buys decoration: whether attendance is genuinely optional and how you say that out loud, who pays, and how the people not in the building take part. Ganesh Chaturthi 2026 is **Monday 14 September**, visarjan is **Friday 25 September**, and most offices use three of those ten days.

The planning window is what teams get wrong. SubhSandesh's only measured festival — Raksha Bandhan, **n = 89 pages** — has a **median lead time of 0 days**, and not one of the 89 was built more than seven days ahead. Meanwhile **49.6% of all page views arrive on a phone** (22,817 of 46,005), which is what a colleague in another city is holding while your aarti happens.

Below: attendance, funding, the three ways to take part, and where this goes wrong.

## What an office celebration involves, and how long it runs

An office Ganesh Chaturthi celebration is a workplace installation of a Ganesh idol with a fixed daily ritual — normally one aarti and prasad — held for a set number of days and closed with visarjan. It is a scheduled organisational event that happens to be religious.

In 2026 the festival runs Monday 14 September to Anant Chaturdashi on Friday 25 September. Almost no office runs all ten days; the traditional shortened forms are 1.5, 3, 5 and 7 days, and three is the usual choice, fitting one working week.

## Is attending optional? 37 employees named attendance pressure and personal sacrifice

Nominally, yes — but a request from the person who writes your appraisal is not received as one.

Junhyok Yim and colleagues, in a paper accepted at the *Journal of Management*, [asked 37 employees what was good and bad about the last workplace celebration they attended](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/10210544/1/Rituals%20JoM_Final%20Pre_proof.pdf). Those 37 gave 105 distinct negative responses across seven categories.

The largest was **require personal sacrifices, at 36 mentions** — the quote given is "having to be at a work event on Friday night". **Exclusion** came second at 20. **Encourage inauthenticity** drew 13, including "Had to act sad that people were leaving when I did not really care". **Attendance pressure** was named five times, once simply as "Attendance was pressured".

Two field studies followed (**n = 90** at one company holiday party, **n = 497** across six ritual types): positive experiences raised engagement, negative ones significantly diminished it. The samples are American, British and German, the authors cannot rule out cultural effects, and none concerns a religious festival — a warning about the mechanism, not a measurement of Indian offices.

So put "optional" in writing, from the organiser rather than the reporting manager, and keep the aarti off a standing meeting slot.

## Who pays, and what that does to the person who did not want to come

Four models. The money matters less than what each makes visible. The rupee figures are **illustrative ranges, not sourced figures**; real costs vary by city and idol size.

### 1. The company pays, everyone is invited

Nothing to the individual, and the only model where declining is genuinely free: there is no ledger with your name missing from it.

### 2. A voluntary collection

Perhaps ₹200–500, illustrative. The amount is not the problem; a contribution sheet is a public document, so a colleague who does not observe the festival declines in front of the list.

### 3. The organiser or team lead pays personally

Nothing to the individual, and that is the trap. Money from a senior person's own pocket creates an obligation no company budget does, and it lands hardest on their reports.

### 4. No money changes hands

A borrowed idol, prasad people bring if they want to, one aarti. Least impressive, and the only model with no financial opt-out to be seen refusing.

The rule from all four: make the opt-out invisible, so nobody can audit who said no.

## Three ways a team can take part, compared

The right-hand column is SubhSandesh's own data, measured 2026-09-09 platform-wide across all 15 page types, because no Ganesh page-creation figure exists — that template only went live this week.

| How the team takes part | Who it reaches | Effort | Is declining visible? | First-party signal (platform-wide) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Idol in the office, daily aarti | Whoever is in that building | 3–5 days of upkeep, one named owner | Highly — you are in the room or you are not | Not measured |
| Video-call aarti at a fixed time | Anyone with a link | 20 minutes, once | Moderately — a camera staying off is legible | Not measured |
| A shareable page each person opens when they choose | Any city, any timezone | 8–10 minutes to build | No — opening a link is private | 49.6% of views on a phone; 42.0% password-protected before sharing |

The fourth column is what listicles leave out. Row three is where [the Ganesh Chaturthi page the recipient performs themselves](/happy-ganesh-chaturthi) fits — they offer the durva, kumkum, flowers and modak, then write their own prarthana back.

## The colleague who does not celebrate: exclusion was the second most-cited complaint

Twenty of those 105 negative responses were exclusion, and the quote is about invitation lists: "some employees invited, and some were not, thus creating a feeling of disparity". The ordinary failure is a list, not hostility.

A religious festival in a mixed workplace has a quieter version: nobody is left off, but the celebration assumes a tradition, and a colleague who does not share it must perform interest or visibly abstain. Yim's **encourage inauthenticity** category, 13 mentions, is that cost.

Two things help without diluting anything: say what the festival is rather than assuming it, and give the ritual a start and end time, so not attending means arriving later rather than making a statement.

On time off, assert nothing. Whether 14 September is a working day depends on your state and your employer's leave policy rather than one national rule, and it varies.

## How a distributed team takes part when the idol sits in one building

Badly, unless someone designs for it — and the person you most want to include is the one most likely to opt out.

Laura Urrila and colleagues, in the *Journal of Vocational Behavior* in 2025, ran [32 interviews with 16 expert employees about belonging in hybrid work](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvb.2025.104096). Employees who lacked a strong sense of belonging *avoided* the office, having felt lonely there before and recounting exclusion from informal gatherings such as lunches. They also felt less lonely knowing everyone else was at home.

Sixteen people in Finland supports no rate, but the asymmetry is the point: nine in a room and three on a screen is worse for those three than a celebration nobody attends in person.

Jakob Lauring and Charlotte Jonasson's [model of inclusiveness in virtual work](https://pure.au.dk/ws/files/381806371/Lauring_2023_How_is_work_group_inclusiveness_influenced.pdf), in *Human Resource Management Review* in 2023, adds the counter-intuitive half: *diffuse* social distance, spread neutrally across everyone, counters the effect of *targeted* distance aimed at dissimilar colleagues, because "the social requirement for conformity and the struggles for status positions are less prominent" online.

That is a proposition rather than a tested result, and their first one runs the other way for group belonging. Still, an online celebration is flatter: nobody sees who skipped. Run the aarti on the call at a time that suits the furthest timezone, then give everyone something to open alone — the [step-by-step guide to building a Ganesh Chaturthi page](/guides/happy-ganesh-chaturthi) covers that half.

## Start planning on 9 September, because the data says almost nobody does

Five days out is already late, and the only festival SubhSandesh has measured says nobody plans further ahead than that.

Across both rakhi collections, **n = 89 pages**, build date against festival date in IST calendar days: **median lead time 0 days**. Forty-four were built on the day itself (49.4%), only six four or more days ahead (6.7%), and not one exceeded seven days.

Two disclosures this number needs. **It is Raksha Bandhan, not Ganesh Chaturthi** — a different festival, and a one-day one, where Ganesh Chaturthi runs ten days to Anant Chaturdashi, so the shape is suggestive rather than measured here. And **n = 89 is small**: it supports no per-template or per-region rate, and no count of Ganesh pages can be projected from it.

It is still the right number for an organiser: a distributed team cannot be assembled on four days' notice, and nobody tries.

Michael Højlund Larsen's four-month study of workplace rituals, [published open-access in *Management Revue* in December 2025](https://www.imrpress.com/journal/MREV/36/4/10.31083/MRev49103), found success depended on a "master of the ritual" — one named person, not a team. Put a name on the aarti slot.

## Where this goes wrong, including where a page is the wrong tool

Larsen's leaders called the first attempts "extremely awkward" and "a waste of time", and that only faded with repetition a once-a-year celebration never gets. His other finding cuts deeper: the *self-created* rituals produced more joy than the predefined one, so a celebration a team designs beats one it is handed.

And the honest limit. A page cannot hand anyone a modak, cannot stand at the mandap for you, and should not be bulk-sent: 42.0% of creators password-protect a page before sharing, which means nothing on a link pasted to four hundred people. Occasion-dated pages are **144 of 3,894** — 3.7% of everything built here — so festival page-building is not a mass behaviour, and claiming otherwise would be a lie.

## Watch the page get built

Ninety seconds, start to finish — the aarti going round, the five offerings, and the box at the end where they write a line back to you: [Ganesh Chaturthi Wishes Online — Full Walkthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mpWiv5T59QY). More page walkthroughs on Instagram: [@subhsandesh_official](https://www.instagram.com/subhsandesh_official).

## Sources

- Yim, J. et al. [Is Everyone Having a Good Time? Complex Organizational Rituals](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/10210544/1/Rituals%20JoM_Final%20Pre_proof.pdf). Accepted, *Journal of Management*; pre-proof, UCL Discovery.
- Urrila, L. et al. (3 February 2025). [Sense of belonging in hybrid work settings](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvb.2025.104096). *Journal of Vocational Behavior* 157, 104096.
- Lauring, J. & Jonasson, C. (26 August 2022). [Work group inclusiveness and virtual work](https://pure.au.dk/ws/files/381806371/Lauring_2023_How_is_work_group_inclusiveness_influenced.pdf). *Human Resource Management Review* 33(1), 100930.
- Larsen, M. H. (15 December 2025). [Rituals and Ritual-like Activities in the Workplace](https://www.imrpress.com/journal/MREV/36/4/10.31083/MRev49103). *Management Revue* 36(4), 49103.

sources.stat: Study 1 (inductive): 37 respondents produced 105 unique negative responses (2.84 per respondent) about their most recent workplace celebration, coded into seven categories with these frequencies — require personal sacrifices (36, e.g. "having to be at a work event on Friday night"), exclusion (20, e.g. "some employees invited, and some were not, thus creating a feeling of disparity"), hinder organizational functioning (16), underappreciation (13), encourage inauthenticity (13, e.g. "Had to act sad that people were leaving when I did not really care"), attendance pressure (5, e.g. "Attendance was pressured"), facilitate unprofessionalism (2). Study 3: US professional MBA students, workplace holiday parties, final sample n=90 (response rate 78.26%). Study 4: employees in Germany via Prolific, six complex ritual types, n=497. Headline: positive ritual experiences raise engagement and predict helping, loyal boosterism and lower job-search behaviour, and negative experiences significantly diminish that effect. Authors' own limitation, quoted: data span "US, UK, and Germany" and "we cannot rule out potential cultural effects", noting perceptions "in more collectivistic cultures may differ significantly". Accepted for publication at Journal of Management; final pre-proof read in FULL (open copy, UCL Discovery institutional repository). The pre-proof carries no publication date, so publishedDate is omitted rather than guessed.

Qualitative study of belonging in hybrid work: 32 interviews at two time points between 2020 and 2022 with 16 expert employees. Findings used: employees lacking a strong sense of belonging avoided going to the office in the hybrid model, reported having previously felt lonely at work, and "recounted instances of categorical and subtle exclusion of colleagues from informal gatherings such as lunching"; they "also felt less lonely when they knew that everyone else was at home alone, too". Also: interviewees described "a sense of drifting apart from colleagues", and time with family or friends outside work "could not replace meaningful social interaction with work colleagues". CC BY 4.0. Full text read via the University of Vaasa open repository copy (osuva.uwasa.fi), which is the same CC BY article the DOI resolves to; ScienceDirect itself returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher (bot block, not a paywall). n=16 is small and qualitative — cited for mechanism only, no rate derived.

Conceptual/theoretical paper (propositions, no empirical test) distinguishing "targeted social distance (towards dissimilar work group members)" from "diffuse social distance (of a more neutral character between all work group members)". Proposition 2, used in the post: "Diffuse social distance will substantially counter the moderately negative effect of targeted social distance on the personal experience of socio-emotional individual oriented inclusion", because "the social requirement for conformity and the struggles for status positions are less prominent under conditions with diffuse social distance" and "the general neutrality with regard to group membership in the online environment could be an advantage for minorities". Proposition 1 runs the other way (diffuse distance substantially increases the negative effect at group level) and the post says so. CC BY; full text read via the Aarhus University open repository copy.

Four-month longitudinal study of workplace rituals with two groups of experienced leaders in a leadership programme (19 of 23 in the Ritual group and 17 of 23 in the Ritual-like group completed the questionnaire), plus group interviews. Findings used: "The success of these rituals was contingent on the involvement of a 'master of the ritual' and the avoidance of perceived awkwardness in the early stages"; participant quotes "The first 2-3 times it is extremely awkward, but now it gives a feeling of togetherness, joy", "In the beginning I thought it was a waste of time", and "too spiritual"; and "a simple, predefined group ritual enhanced feelings of inner peace, readiness, and togetherness, whereas higher-arousal feelings of joy and energy were associated with a self-created ritual". Open access under CC BY 4.0; full text read.

auditReport.honestAssessment: It is the only page on this SERP that treats an office religious festival as an organisational-design problem rather than an ideas catalogue: all ten competing results are decoration, rangoli, modak and team-building lists, eight of them content marketing attached to an event agency, gifting vendor or coworking operator, and not one addresses who is expected to attend, who pays, what a non-observant colleague does during an aarti, or how a distributed team participates. The defensible material is the combination an answer engine cannot get elsewhere — Yim et al.'s seven negative ritual experiences with their frequencies (exclusion 20, attendance pressure 5, personal sacrifices 36), Lauring and Jonasson's counter-intuitive proposition that online neutrality can help a minority group member, and SubhSandesh's own n=89 lead-time measurement — plus the 'is declining visible?' table column, which no competitor has. Real weaknesses: the ritual research is American, British, German and Finnish and none of it is about a religious festival in an Indian office, so every applied claim is a mechanism argument rather than a measurement; the n=89 lead-time figure is Raksha Bandhan, not Ganesh Chaturthi, and 89 is small; the cost figures are labelled illustrative because no dated source for Indian office celebration costs was found; and Phase 1 could not capture the AI Overview or People-Also-Ask blocks, because the WebSearch tool exposes neither and every India-localised path was rate-limited, so the SERP picture is US-localised and incomplete. Domain authority against entrenched event-agency and HR-vendor content is unknown and unaddressed by anything in this post; no ranking outcome is predicted.
